title: He Was Supposed to Be at War That Year. He Painted a Tree and Quit His Own Group Instead.
standfirst: Pyotr Konchalovsky's service record puts him in an artillery unit for the entire year this canvas is dated. The record also has him walking out on the chairmanship of the avant-garde group he had led for six years — and it leaves the rest, including how a tree got painted in between, unexplained.

sections.heading: A Soldier's Date on a Studio Canvas
sections.body: The catalogue dates this picture to 1916. Konchalovsky's own service record places him in an artillery unit for that whole year: the [Russian Wikipedia entry](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%9A%D0%BE%D0%BD%D1%87%D0%B0%D0%BB%D0%BE%D0%B2%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B8%D0%B9,_%D0%9F%D1%91%D1%82%D1%80_%D0%9F%D0%B5%D1%82%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%B8%D1%87) and a [biography from the Russian Avant-Garde project](https://rusavangard.ru/online/biographies/konchalovskiy-pyetr-petrovich/) both give his active duty as running from 1914 to 1917, with the rank of praporshchik — a junior officer, roughly a second lieutenant — and an interruption only for medical treatment. The [English-language account of his career](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyotr_Konchalovsky) gives a shorter war, ending his service in 1916 rather than 1917. The two records disagree by a year, and neither one explains where, in whichever year it actually was, he found a studio to paint a tree.

sections.heading: He Chaired the Group He Was About to Leave
sections.body: Six years before this canvas is dated, Konchalovsky had been a founder of the Knave of Diamonds and its first elected chairman. The group, which grew out of a December 1910 exhibition in Moscow, set out, according to the [history of the association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knave_of_Diamonds_%28arts_association%29), to fuse Paul Cézanne's structure with Russian folk sources — icon painting, the lubok print, the painted shop sign — rather than import a Western style wholesale. 1916 was also the year Konchalovsky stepped down: he and fellow founder Ilya Mashkov left the leadership, handing the chair to Aleksandr Kuprin. By October 1917 the chair had passed again, to Kazimir Malevich, whose Suprematism had nothing to do with Cézanne or the lubok, and within two months the group Konchalovsky had chaired for six years dissolved itself. Whatever this tree was arguing for, it was painted at the exact point where its maker had stopped running the argument.

sections.heading: A Label Borrowed From Three Years Earlier
sections.body: The corpus files this work under Cubism. [Britannica's account](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Pyotr-Petrovich-Konchalovsky) of Konchalovsky's career has his style moving, across the 1910s, from Cézannism into primitivism and "then with Cubism" — a sequence with no year attached to the last step. The [biography from the Russian Avant-Garde project](https://rusavangard.ru/online/biographies/konchalovskiy-pyetr-petrovich/) dates the actual technical turn earlier: the collage effects, the imitation of surface texture, the deliberately stacked and clashing forms that read as cubist in his work, it says, appear by 1912 and 1913, in paintings titled Beer and Vobla and Dry Paints. That is three or four years, and most of a world war, before this tree. By 1916 that vocabulary was not something Konchalovsky was discovering. It was one he already had, pointed at a new subject while, on paper, he was meant to be in uniform.

sections.heading: No One Has Written a Sentence About This Particular Tree
sections.body: Search the record for this specific picture and it comes back empty. The agaves Konchalovsky is known to have painted the same year are logged in the [Russian Wikipedia entry](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%9A%D0%BE%D0%BD%D1%87%D0%B0%D0%BB%D0%BE%D0%B2%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B8%D0%B9,_%D0%9F%D1%91%D1%82%D1%80_%D0%9F%D0%B5%D1%82%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%B8%D1%87) with a named home, the State Tretyakov Gallery, and a reproducible date. The tree carries no comparable trail: no exhibition, no recorded owner, nothing beyond [WikiArt's own catalogue entry](https://www.wikiart.org/en/pyotr-konchalovsky/a-tree-1916) for it. That gap is not unusual on its own — [Konchalovsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyotr_Konchalovsky) is credited with more than five thousand works across a sixty-year career, and most of them were never going to be written about one by one — but it means anything said about this canvas beyond its date and its borrowed label is reaching past what the record actually holds.

sections.heading: The Grandsons Who Took the Family Into Cinema
sections.body: In 1902 Konchalovsky married Olga Surikova, daughter of the history painter Vasily Surikov — marrying into one of the most decorated names in Russian painting before he had made one for himself. [Their daughter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyotr_Konchalovsky), the writer Natalya Konchalovskaya, later married the poet Sergei Mikhalkov, who wrote the words to two versions of the Soviet national anthem and, decades later, to Russia's post-Soviet one, making Konchalovsky father-in-law to the man who wrote his country's anthem three times over. The couple's two sons went into film rather than poetry or paint: Andrei took his mother's surname, Konchalovsky, and has directed since the 1960s; his brother, Nikita Mikhalkov, directed the 1994 film Burnt by the Sun, which won the Oscar for best foreign-language film. Konchalovsky himself spent his later decades moving away from the Cézanne he had once idolised, becoming, after the Second World War, a member of the USSR Academy of Fine Arts and a People's Artist of the RSFSR for the ceremonial portraits that replaced his cubist trees. A century on, the name carries further in Russian cinema than in Russian painting.
